about.title: Coachella Product Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Defective products cause harm in ordinary settings throughout Coachella — a malfunctioning tool on a Grapefruit Boulevard job site, a faulty auto part that fails while driving near Cesar Chavez Street, or a household appliance that catches fire in a home off Van Buren Street. California law generally treats these cases under strict liability, meaning an injured person often doesn't need to prove the company was careless, only that the product itself was defective and that the defect caused harm. That can apply to a manufacturing flaw, a design problem, or a missing warning. Coachella's mix of agricultural work, warehousing, and everyday consumer use means residents encounter a wide range of products daily, and when one fails, the consequences can be serious. LawProactive connects injured residents with an independent attorney, free of charge, so they can find out what their options may be. There's no obligation, and the attorneys in this network work on contingency — no fee unless there's a recovery. Preserving the product itself is important, so don't discard or repair it before speaking with someone.

items.title: Strict Liability May Apply
items.desc: Under California law, you often don't have to prove a company was negligent — just that the product was defective and caused your injury. This can make certain claims more direct to pursue.

items.title: Multiple Parties May Be Responsible
items.desc: Manufacturers, distributors, and retailers can all potentially share liability for a defective product. An attorney can help identify every party connected to what happened to you.

items.title: Guidance on Preserving Evidence
items.desc: Because the product itself is often the most important piece of evidence, an attorney can advise you early on how to keep it safe and unaltered.

items.question: What counts as a product defect under California law?
items.answer: There are generally three types: a design defect (the product is inherently unsafe even if made correctly), a manufacturing defect (something went wrong during production), or a warning defect (the product lacked adequate instructions or safety warnings). An independent attorney can help figure out which category applies to your situation.

items.question: I still have the broken product from an incident near Grapefruit Boulevard — should I get rid of it?
items.answer: No, hold onto it. The product itself is often central evidence in these claims, and repairing, discarding, or altering it can make a case much harder to prove. Store it safely and let an attorney review it before you do anything else.

items.question: Does LawProactive charge anything to connect me with an attorney?
items.answer: No, the connection service is free. Attorneys in the network work on contingency, meaning there's no fee unless you recover compensation.
